summary.text: The House of Wisdom, also known as the Grand Library of Baghdad, was a major public academy and intellectual centre in Abbasid-era Baghdad.
It was part of the Translation Movement that turned works from Greek and Syriac into Arabic, though it was unlikely to be the only centre of that work.
Scholars linked to it contributed to philosophy, mathematics, medicine, astronomy, and optics, until it was destroyed in the Mongol siege of Baghdad in 1258.

facts.label: Made a public academy
facts.value: Under the caliph al-Ma'mun, who reigned 813 to 833

facts.label: Peace demand
facts.value: Al-Ma'mun claimed Ptolemy's Almagest after a war with the Eastern Roman Empire

facts.label: Destroyed
facts.value: In 1258, during the Mongol siege of Baghdad

items.prompt: Scholars from Arab, Persian, and other lands kept arriving in Baghdad. What drew them there?

options.label: It held the old Sasanian Imperial Library
It was the capital of the Umayyads in Damascus
It was the capital of the Abbasid Caliphate
It was the only city that had a library

items.explain: The House of Wisdom was made possible by a steady flow of scholars to Baghdad, owing to the city's position as capital of the Abbasid Caliphate. Its cosmopolitan population helped too.

items.prompt: A tour guide says every Greek work translated into Arabic was done inside the House of Wisdom. Why is that unlikely?

options.label: Major translation efforts arose in Cairo and Damascus even earlier
Greek works were never translated into Arabic at all
Translators worked only in private homes and never in groups
The House of Wisdom was founded after the Mongol siege

items.explain: The House of Wisdom was part of the wider Translation Movement, but it is unlikely to have been its sole centre, since major translation efforts arose in Cairo and Damascus even earlier.

items.prompt: The Abbasids set up a palace library to translate foreign works into Arabic. Whose practice were they following?

options.label: The Byzantine emperors
The Sasanian Empire
The Roman Republic
The Chinese court

items.explain: The Abbasid dynasty had a strong Persian bent and adopted many Sasanian practices, including translating foreign works. Al-Mansur founded a palace library modelled after the Sasanian Imperial Library.

items.prompt: After a war, al-Ma'mun claimed Ptolemy's Almagest as a condition for peace with the Eastern Roman Empire. What does that show about his society?

options.label: Its rulers cared very little for learning of any kind
Its scholars were forced to work for the army
It had no libraries of its own at that time
Knowledge was prized so highly that texts could beat riches

items.explain: Scientific knowledge was considered so valuable that books and ancient texts were sometimes preferred as war booty over riches, and the Almagest is one example.

items.prompt: In Baghdad, the court needs an official calendar kept and a large building designed. Whom would it most likely call on?

options.label: Merchants who funded the House of Wisdom
Soldiers who guarded the city
Scholars of the House of Wisdom
Poets of the caliph's court

items.explain: The House of Wisdom was more than an academic centre. Its scholars usually doubled as engineers and architects on major construction projects, kept accurate official calendars, and were public servants.

items.prompt: A young person in Abbasid Baghdad hopes to become a scholar or translator. What can they expect?

options.label: An easy living and a high place in society
Poverty, since only the caliph could pay scholars
A ban on working for merchants or soldiers
Forced service in the army after their studies

items.explain: It was easy for scholars and translators to make a living, and an academic life indicated high status. Support came from the caliph, and also from merchants and the military.
